text: <highlight>Blind XSS</highlight> is a form of Stored XSS where the malicious payload is executed in a high-privileged application or page that the attacker cannot access. The attacker 'fires and forgets,' waiting for a callback from a victim (usually an administrator) who views the stored data in an internal dashboard.

title: Why alert() Often Fails in Blind Scenarios
items: If you use <highlight>alert()</highlight>, the popup triggers on the Admin's screen, not yours.
The Admin will immediately know they are under attack and close the ticket/report.
To succeed, you need an <highlight>Out-of-Band (OOB)</highlight> callback to confirm execution.

text: The goal is to be <highlight>silent</highlight>. The payload reaches out to the attacker's server, carrying the sensitive session cookie as a URL parameter. The Admin sees nothing unusual on their dashboard while their session is being hijacked.

title: Execution Steps
items: **Identify Entry Point:** Find a form that an admin must eventually review (Support Tickets, Bug Reports, Contact Forms).
**Deploy Listener:** Set up <highlight>Netcat</highlight>, <highlight>Python SimpleHTTPServer</highlight>, or a tool like <highlight>XSS Hunter</highlight>.
**Inject Payload:** Submit the callback script into the form.
**Wait:** Execution only happens when the Admin logs in and views your specific entry.
**Capture:** Check logs for an incoming GET request containing a Base64 string.

text: The main difference between Blind and normal Stored XSS is the <highlight>Visibility</highlight>. In normal Stored XSS, you can verify the exploit yourself. In Blind XSS, you rely entirely on your <highlight>external listener</highlight> to know if the attack was successful.
